A.explanation: Acceleration of free fall is a vector, but not because its magnitude is constant. It is a vector because it has magnitude and direction vertically downwards.

B.explanation: Temperature in $^{\circ}\text{C}$ can be positive or negative but has no direction in space, so it is a scalar quantity.

C.explanation: Time has only magnitude and always increases, but always increasing is not the same as having a vector direction, so time is a scalar.

D.explanation: Weight is the gravitational force $W = mg$ on a mass and acts vertically downwards, so it has both magnitude and direction.

hints: Look at the word after because in each statement and ask whether having constant magnitude, having a sign, or going forwards is the test for a vector.
Recall that a vector quantity must need both a magnitude and a direction in space, such as downwards or along a displacement.
Check weight against that test: it has a value in newtons and it pulls towards the centre of the Earth.
walkthrough: State the definition: a scalar has magnitude only, while a vector has both magnitude and direction.
Test option A: acceleration of free fall $g$ is about $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards, so it is a vector, but constant magnitude alone does not make a quantity a vector.
Test option B: temperature in $^{\circ}\text{C}$ is measured by a number only. A minus sign means colder than $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, not a direction in space, so it is a scalar.
Test option C: time is measured by a duration in $\text{s}$. Saying it goes forwards describes that it increases, not that it points in a spatial direction, so it is a scalar.
Test option D: weight is a force with magnitude in $\text{N}$ and a clear direction towards the Earth, so it satisfies both parts of the vector definition. This is option D.
